ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
One commercially available ten-button lock may be opened by depressing -- in any order -- the correct five buttons. The sample shown below has $\{1, 2, 3, 6, 9\}$ as its combination. Suppose that these locks are redesigned so that sets of as many as nine buttons or as few as one button could serve as combinations. How many additional combinations would this allow?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: The image shows a ten-button lock, with the buttons numbered from 1 to 10; in the example, the buttons that are pressed/blackened are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, corresponding to a five-button combination. Because the problem states that the buttons can be pressed “in any order,” a combination is determined only by the set of selected buttons, and order is not counted. The original lock allowed only exactly 5 buttons to be selected from the 10 buttons as a combination, so the original number of combinations was C(10,5)=252. After the redesign, combination sizes from 1 button to 9 buttons are allowed, that is, among all subsets of the 10 buttons, the empty set and the full set are excluded, so the new total number of combinations is 2^10-2=1022. The problem asks how many combinations were added, so subtract the original number of combinations from the new number of combinations: 1022-252=770.

method.method_draft: Identify that a combination is a subset of buttons because order does not matter. From the text, the original lock permits only 5-button combinations among 10 buttons, so count the old possibilities as C(10,5). The redesign permits any subset size from 1 through 9, so count the new possibilities as sum_{k=1}^9 C(10,k), equivalently all subsets of 10 except the empty set and the full 10-button set: 2^10 - 2. Subtract the old count: (2^10 - 2) - C(10,5) = 1022 - 252 = 770.
